key_terms.meaning: A relation ≤ on a set P that is reflexive (a ≤ a), antisymmetric (a ≤ b and b ≤ a → a = b) and transitive (a ≤ b, b ≤ c → a ≤ c).
A pair (P, ≤) where P is a nonempty set and ≤ is a partial order on P.
The smallest element of P that is ≥ both a and b; exists only when the poset allows it.
The largest element of P that is ≤ both a and b.
A poset in which every pair of elements has both a join and a meet inside the set.
A set L with two binary operations ∨ and ∧ that are idempotent, commutative, associative and satisfy absorption; a ≤ b means a ∧ b = a.
Swapping ∨ with ∧ and ≤ with ≥ in any true lattice statement gives another true statement.
a ∨ (a ∧ b) = a and a ∧ (a ∨ b) = a, true in every lattice.
A nonempty subset S of a lattice L such that a, b ∈ S implies a ∨ b ∈ S and a ∧ b ∈ S, with the joins and meets computed in L.
L₁ × L₂ with operations done coordinatewise: (a₁,b₁) ∨ (a₂,b₂) = (a₁∨a₂, b₁∨b₂) and similarly for ∧.
A map h: L₁ → L₂ with h(a ∨ b) = h(a) ∨ h(b) and h(a ∧ b) = h(a) ∧ h(b) for all a, b.
A lattice with a least element 0 (zero) and a greatest element 1 (unit), so 0 ≤ a ≤ 1 for every a.
In a bounded lattice, b is a complement of a when a ∨ b = 1 and a ∧ b = 0.
A bounded lattice in which every element has at least one complement.
A lattice where a ∧ (b ∨ c) = (a ∧ b) ∨ (a ∧ c) and the dual law a ∨ (b ∧ c) = (a ∨ b) ∧ (a ∨ c) hold.
A bounded, complemented, distributive lattice, written (B, ∨, ∧, ′, 0, 1), with ′ the complement operation.
(a ∨ b)′ = a′ ∧ b′ and (a ∧ b)′ = a′ ∨ b′, valid in every Boolean algebra.
For n variables, a product of all n variables, each either plain or complemented; equals 1 at exactly one row of the truth table.
A sum of all n variables, each either plain or complemented; equals 0 at exactly one row of the truth table.
Disjunctive normal form is a sum (OR) of product terms; conjunctive normal form is a product (AND) of sum terms.
A subset S of a Boolean algebra B with 0, 1 ∈ S, closed under ∨, ∧ and ′.
A map h: B₁ → B₂ with h(a ∨ b) = h(a) ∨ h(b), h(a ∧ b) = h(a) ∧ h(b), h(a′) = (h(a))′ and h(0) = 0, h(1) = 1.

takeaways: A lattice is one idea seen twice: a poset with pairwise joins and meets, or a set with two well-behaved operations, and the two views give the same objects.
The order and the operations translate into each other by the rule a ≤ b ⇔ a ∧ b = a ⇔ a ∨ b = b, so you can prove facts in whichever language is easier.
Idempotent, commutative, associative and absorption laws hold in every lattice and are all you need to do algebra with ∨ and ∧.
A sublattice must be closed under join and meet computed in the big lattice; closure under one operation alone is not enough.
Products and homomorphisms build new lattices from old ones and preserve exactly the structure the operations carry.
Adding boundedness, complements and distributivity one by one leads to the Boolean lattice, where every element has a well-defined complement.
Boolean algebra is a compact axiom system: from a handful of identities you can derive De Morgan's laws, the 0–1 rules and the uniqueness of complement.
Every Boolean function becomes a Boolean polynomial, and the truth table hands you the DNF (from the 1-rows) and the CNF (from the 0-rows) directly.
Sub-Boolean algebras and Boolean homomorphisms are the structural tools: they let you compare algebras and carry identities from one to another.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are mostly proofs from the axioms plus one worked example: state the definitions, verify closure or a law line by line, then confirm with a small Hasse diagram or truth table.

bank.q: Define a partial order and a poset. Define a lattice as a poset, and state the join and meet axioms of a lattice as an algebraic system.
outline: Reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive conditions with symbols
LUB and GLB definition for a pair a, b
Closure, idempotent, commutative, associative, absorption laws
One example (divisors of 12 under divisibility) and one non-example (the two-element poset with no join)

bank.q: Explain why a lattice can be described both as a poset and as an algebraic system. Show how the partial order is recovered from the operations and how the operations are recovered from the order.
outline: Define a ≤ b by a ∧ b = a and prove this is a partial order
Show LUB of a, b is a ∨ b and GLB is a ∧ b
Derive idempotent and absorption laws from the order definition
State the equivalence theorem and note it lets you swap viewpoints in proofs

bank.q: State the idempotent, commutative, associative and absorption laws for lattices, and prove the absorption law a ∨ (a ∧ b) = a from the poset definition.
outline: All four laws with symbols and variable meanings
Use a ∧ b ≤ a, so a is an upper bound of a and a ∧ b
a is the least upper bound because a ∨ (a ∧ b) ≤ a
Combine with a ≤ a ∨ (a ∧ b) and antisymmetry

bank.q: Define sublattice, bounded lattice, complemented lattice and distributive lattice. Give one example of each and one lattice that is bounded but not complemented.
outline: Closure of a nonempty subset under both operations
Bounds 0 and 1 with 0 ≤ a ≤ 1
Complement condition a ∨ b = 1 and a ∧ b = 0
Distributive identities, plus the chain 0 < a < 1 as a bounded, non-complemented example

bank.q: Define a Boolean algebra as an algebraic system and list its laws. Explain why every Boolean algebra is a bounded distributive complemented lattice.
outline: Carrier B, operations ∨, ∧, ′, constants 0 and 1
Idempotent, commutative, associative, absorption, distributive laws
Complement laws a ∨ a′ = 1, a ∧ a′ = 0
Show the derived order a ≤ b ⇔ a ∧ b = a makes B a lattice, then a Boolean lattice

bank.q: For the poset of divisors of 30 under divisibility, find the join and meet of every pair, identify all sublattices of size 4, and decide whether the lattice is bounded, complemented and distributive.
outline: Join is lcm, meet is gcd
Hasse diagram with 1 at the bottom and 30 at the top
Sublattice test by closure under lcm and gcd
Complement of d is 30/d, so complemented; check distributivity by the gcd/lcm identity

bank.q: Take L₁ as the chain 0 < 1 and L₂ as the four-element Boolean lattice. Construct the direct product L₁ × L₂, draw its Hasse diagram, and define a homomorphism from it onto L₁, verifying the homomorphism conditions.
outline: Elements are ordered pairs, operations coordinatewise
Eight elements with order (a,b) ≤ (a′,b′) iff a ≤ a′ and b ≤ b′
Map to first coordinate; check join, meet are preserved
Note the map is onto but not one-one, so not an isomorphism

bank.q: A Boolean function of three variables x, y, z is 1 exactly on the rows 011, 101, 110, 111. Write its DNF using minterms and its CNF using maxterms, and simplify the DNF.
outline: Minterms x′yz, xy′z, xyz′, xyz
CNF from the four 0-rows using maxterms
Group terms to get xy + x′yz + xy′z and simplify to xy + yz + xz style result
Check simplification against the original truth table

bank.q: Using the laws of Boolean algebra, simplify the polynomial (a ∧ b′) ∨ (a ∧ b) ∨ (a′ ∧ b) and prove each step names a law.
outline: Distributive law to factor a out of the first two terms
Complement law a ∧ (b ∨ b′) = a ∧ 1 = a
Absorption or distribution to reach a ∨ b
Justify every identity used by name

bank.q: Let B be the power set of {1, 2, 3} under union, intersection and complement. Decide whether {∅, {1}, {1,2,3}} and {∅, {1}, {2}, {1,2,3}} are sub-Boolean algebras, and whether the map sending each set to its size is a Boolean homomorphism.
outline: Closure under union and intersection first
Complement of {1} must lie in the subset
Size map fails: sizes add under union, and 0 and 1 are not preserved in the required sense
Conclusion: first is not closed, second is a sub-Boolean algebra

bank.q: Prove that a lattice is distributive if and only if every element has at most one complement in a bounded lattice setting, and use this to show that the diamond lattice M₅ is not distributive.
outline: Assume distributive; suppose b and c both complement a
Compute b = b ∧ 1 = b ∧ (a ∨ c) and distribute
Use a ∧ b = 0 and a ∨ b = 1 to reduce to c
In M₅ the middle element has two complements, so no distributivity
Careful statement of the lattice-theoretic criterion used

bank.q: Prove De Morgan's laws (a ∨ b)′ = a′ ∧ b′ and (a ∧ b)′ = a′ ∨ b′ from the Boolean algebra axioms, and explain why the proof needs distributivity and uniqueness of complement.
outline: Show (a ∨ b) ∨ (a′ ∧ b′) = 1 by distribution
Show (a ∨ b) ∧ (a′ ∧ b′) = 0
Invoke uniqueness of complement in a distributive complemented lattice
Dual argument for the second law

bank.q: Show that every Boolean function of n variables has a DNF representation, that the minterm expansion is unique up to the order of terms, and explain why each minterm is 1 on exactly one assignment.
outline: Each minterm is a product of n literals, one per variable
Evaluate a minterm on an assignment: it is 1 only if each literal matches
Sum over the 1-rows reproduces the function value on every row
Uniqueness: two different sets of minterms differ on some row

bank.q: Let h: B₁ → B₂ be a Boolean homomorphism. Prove that h(0) = 0, h(1) = 1, and that the image h(B₁) is a sub-Boolean algebra of B₂. Give an example of a lattice homomorphism that is not a Boolean homomorphism.
outline: Preservation of join, meet, complement and both constants
Image contains 0 and 1, closed under the three operations
Counterexample: a monotone map on a bounded lattice that preserves join and meet but not complement
Distinguish lattice homomorphism from Boolean homomorphism

glossary.def: A reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive relation on a set.
A set together with a partial order on it.
Elements a, b with a ≤ b or b ≤ a; otherwise they are incomparable.
A drawing of a finite poset with elements as dots, covering pairs joined upward, and no arrows or loops.
An element u with a ≤ u and b ≤ u for the pair under study.
The smallest of all upper bounds of a pair; written a ∨ b.
The largest of all lower bounds of a pair; written a ∧ b.
Another name for the least upper bound operation ∨.
Another name for the greatest lower bound operation ∧.
A poset in which every pair of elements has a join and a meet, or equivalently a set with two idempotent, commutative, associative, absorbing operations.
A nonempty subset closed under the join and meet of the whole lattice.
The lattice of ordered pairs from two lattices, with operations applied coordinate by coordinate.
A map preserving join and meet for all pairs of elements.
A bijective lattice homomorphism; the two lattices then have identical structure.
A lattice possessing a least element 0 and a greatest element 1.
An element b with a ∨ b = 1 and a ∧ b = 0 for a given a.
A bounded lattice in which every element has at least one complement.
A lattice satisfying a ∧ (b ∨ c) = (a ∧ b) ∨ (a ∧ c) and its dual.
A bounded, complemented, distributive lattice, or the equivalent axiom system (B, ∨, ∧, ′, 0, 1).
A map from {0,1}ⁿ to {0,1}, usually given by a truth table.
An expression built from variables and the constants 0, 1 using ∨, ∧ and ′.
A product of all n variables, each plain or complemented, true on exactly one assignment.
A sum of all n variables, each plain or complemented, false on exactly one assignment.
Disjunctive normal form: an OR of AND terms, canonical when all terms are minterms.
Conjunctive normal form: an AND of OR terms, canonical when all terms are maxterms.
A subset containing 0 and 1 and closed under ∨, ∧ and ′.
